children.note: Gross anatomy by region, histology, embryology and neuroanatomy: the structural basis for clinical examination, procedures, imaging and surgery for every doctor in Kenya.
Psychology, sociology and anthropology applied to health: behaviour, development, stress, culture and communication, so Kenyan doctors treat the whole person.

Foundations of how the body works: cells and body fluids, nerve and muscle, blood, heart, circulation and breathing — the basis for understanding anaemia, sickle cell, shock and hypoxia in Kenyan practice.
Foundations of biomolecules, enzymes, vitamins and core energy metabolism, the base for understanding diabetes, malnutrition, G6PD deficiency and sickle cell disease seen in Kenyan practice.
4 courses. Tap a course's arrow to open its map.

children.topic: Year 2 · Body in health and disease

children.note: Advanced systems physiology — kidney, acid–base, gut, endocrine, reproduction, neurophysiology and special senses — underpinning care of diabetes, dehydration, pregnancy and neurological illness in Kenya.

Advanced lipid, amino acid, haem and nucleotide metabolism, molecular biology, hormone signalling and nutrition — linking biochemistry to jaundice, malnutrition, drug action and molecular diagnostics.
Principles of laboratory testing and interpretation of electrolytes, acid–base, renal, liver, glucose, bone and protein tests — the everyday results a doctor in Kenya must read correctly.
Foundations of bacteriology, virology and mycology: microbial structure, growth, genetics, sterilisation, antibiotics and resistance, and key bacterial pathogens seen in Kenyan practice.

Basic immunology: cells and organs of immunity, innate defences, complement, antibodies, antigen presentation, T and B cells, cytokines and tolerance – the basis for understanding infection and vaccines.
Principles of pharmacology — pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, adverse reactions, interactions and autonomic drugs — the basis for safe prescribing by every doctor in Kenya.

The general mechanisms of disease: cell injury, inflammation, repair, circulatory disorders, immune injury and neoplasia. The language every Kenyan clinician needs to reason about TB, malaria, cancer and more.

children.topic: HHP 201 · Haematology and Blood Transfusion I
children.note: Foundations of haematology: blood cell production, haemoglobin, iron, the blood count and film, the anaemias, haemostasis and blood groups. Anaemia from iron lack, malaria and sickle cell is everyday work in Kenya.
8 courses. Tap a course's arrow to open its map.
Advanced clinical chemistry: endocrine function tests, emergencies, tumour markers, drug and toxin testing, body fluids and lab monitoring in pregnancy, newborns, HIV and TB care in Kenya.
Systematic virology and parasitology, systemic mycoses and a systems-based approach to infections, diagnosis and infection control for the common infectious diseases of Kenya.

Immunology applied to disease: immunity to infection, hypersensitivity, autoimmunity, immunodeficiency including HIV, transplantation, tumour immunology, vaccines, immunodiagnostics and immunotherapy.
Systemic pharmacology and chemotherapy: antimicrobials for TB, HIV and malaria, and cardiovascular, respiratory, GI, endocrine and CNS drugs used daily in Kenyan practice.
Foundations of anaesthesia: preoperative assessment, airway skills, monitoring, fluids and the pharmacology of anaesthetic drugs, plus basic life support.

children.topic: HHP 300 · General Pathology (lab and clinical clerkship)
children.note: Hands-on laboratory pathology and systemic pathology of the major organs, linking specimens, stains and cytology to the cancers and infections common in Kenyan wards.

children.topic: HHP 301 · Haematology and Blood Transfusion II
children.note: Clinical haematology: managing sickle cell disease, marrow failure, leukaemias, lymphomas, myeloma, bleeding and clotting disorders, and safe transfusion practice in Kenyan hospitals.

children.topic: HPD 300 · Paediatrics and Child Health I
children.note: Foundations of child health: history and examination, growth, development, nutrition, immunisation, newborn care, fluids and emergency triage (ETAT+, IMNCI) as practised in Kenyan health facilities.

Foundations of obstetrics and gynaecology: pelvic anatomy, reproductive physiology, normal pregnancy, antenatal care, normal labour and puerperium, family planning and genital infections in the Kenyan setting.
9 courses. Tap a course's arrow to open its map.
Foundations of adult internal medicine: clinical method and the common cardiovascular, respiratory, infectious, metabolic and blood diseases a Kenyan doctor manages daily.
Foundations of psychiatry: the psychiatric interview, classification, and diagnosis and treatment of the major mental and substance use disorders common in Kenya.

Foundations of surgery: wound healing, surgical infection, fluids, shock, transfusion, perioperative care, trauma, burns, lumps, hernias, thyroid and breast. Core for every Kenyan doctor facing surgical emergencies.

Foundations of orthopaedics and trauma: examination, fracture description and healing, fracture management and complications, common limb injuries, dislocations, spinal injury, bone and joint infection and TB.

Foundations of radiology: imaging modalities, radiation safety, contrast media and systematic reading of chest, abdominal and skeletal X-rays, plus ultrasound, CT and MRI basics — core for every clinician in Kenya.
Foundations of eye anatomy, optics, examination and the common eye conditions (red eye, cataract, glaucoma, trauma) that a Kenyan doctor must recognise, treat or refer.
Foundations of ear, nose and throat anatomy, examination and the common infections and emergencies (otitis media, epistaxis, tonsillitis, foreign bodies) seen daily in Kenya.
Foundations of public health for Kenya: PHC, the KEPH health system, community strategy, epidemiology, biostatistics, WASH, nutrition, immunisation and disease control.
Ethics, consent, confidentiality, communication, professionalism, KMPDC regulation, Kenyan medical law and patient safety: the rules and values every Kenyan doctor must practise by.
9 courses. Tap a course's arrow to open its map.

children.topic: HPD 500 · Paediatrics and Child Health II
children.note: Clinical paediatrics for the Kenyan hospital: neonatal emergencies, pneumonia, diarrhoea, malnutrition, malaria, HIV, TB, sickle cell, heart and kidney disease and childhood cancers, using the Basic Paediatric Protocols.

Clinical obstetrics and gynaecology: the major causes of maternal death in Kenya (haemorrhage, hypertension, sepsis, obstructed labour), medical disorders in pregnancy, early pregnancy problems, infertility and gynaecological cancers.
Applied community health: health systems, policy, financing, management, screening, outbreak response, HIV/TB/malaria and NCD programmes, occupational health, research and M&E.
3 courses. Tap a course's arrow to open its map.
Applying pharmacology at the bedside: rational prescribing, Kenyan guideline regimens for malaria, HIV, TB and NCDs, poisoning, snakebite and palliative care.
Clinical anaesthesia and critical care: emergency airways, obstetric and paediatric anaesthesia, resuscitation, trauma, transfusion and postoperative care in Kenya.
Medicolegal duties of the doctor in Kenya: documenting injuries (P3, PRC forms), post-mortem changes, identification, wounds, asphyxia, sexual violence, poisoning, ethics and the medicolegal autopsy.
Advanced and emergency internal medicine: neurological, renal, hepatic, endocrine, haematological, rheumatological and toxicological disease, preparing students for internship in Kenya.
Recognition and management of common skin diseases, including tropical, infectious and HIV-related dermatoses and skin signs of systemic disease seen in Kenya.
Advanced and applied psychiatry: child, perinatal and old-age psychiatry, personality, trauma, eating and somatic disorders, emergencies, therapies and Kenyan mental health law.

Advanced and clinical surgery: the acute abdomen, gastrointestinal, hepatobiliary, colorectal, urological, vascular and paediatric surgical conditions as seen in Kenyan hospitals, with emphasis on emergency decisions.

Advanced orthopaedics: nonunion and chronic osteomyelitis, polytrauma, hand, nerve injuries, paediatric orthopaedics, metabolic bone disease, bone tumours, arthritis, back pain, sickle cell bone disease and amputation.

Clinical radiology: choosing and interpreting imaging for chest infections, cardiac, abdominal, genitourinary, obstetric, neuro, trauma, musculoskeletal, breast, oncology and paediatric problems, plus interventional radiology.
Advanced and clinical ophthalmology: retinal, neuro-ophthalmic, paediatric, HIV-related and blinding tropical eye disease, plus community eye health for practice in Kenya.
Advanced ENT and head and neck surgery: complications of ear disease, hearing loss and vertigo, facial palsy, deep neck infections, airway surgery and head and neck cancers common in Kenya.
Oral and dental conditions a doctor must recognise — caries, gum disease, oral infections, HIV lesions, noma, fluorosis and oral cancer — and how to prevent, treat and refer in Kenya.
12 courses. Tap a course's arrow to open its map.

children.note: Standing erect, facing forward, upper limbs by the sides with palms facing forward, feet together and pointing forward.

manas.q: Describe the anatomical position.

children.note: Vertical plane dividing the body into right and left parts; the median (midsagittal) plane passes through the midline.

manas.q: Which plane divides the body into right and left parts?

children.note: Vertical plane dividing the body into anterior and posterior parts; also called the frontal plane.

manas.q: Which plane divides the body into anterior and posterior parts?

children.note: Horizontal plane dividing the body into superior and inferior parts; axial CT images are transverse slices.

manas.q: Which plane divides the body into superior and inferior parts?

children.note: Proximal = nearer the root of a limb or the trunk; distal = farther from it. The elbow is proximal to the wrist.

manas.q: What do proximal and distal mean?

children.note: Flexion decreases the angle between two parts (bending); extension increases it (straightening).

manas.q: What is the difference between flexion and extension?

children.note: Abduction moves away from the median plane, adduction towards it. For fingers the reference is the middle (3rd) digit; for toes the 2nd toe.

manas.q: What is the reference line for abduction of the fingers?

children.note: Supination turns the palm anteriorly (upwards when elbow flexed); pronation turns it posteriorly. Occur at the proximal and distal radioulnar joints.

manas.q: At which joints do supination and pronation occur?

children.topic: 📖 9.5 Types of Body Movements (OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology)

children.note: The anatomical position, body planes, relational terms and joint movements used to describe every structure precisely.
Single layer of flat cells lining alveoli, blood vessels (endothelium) and serous cavities (mesothelium); suited to diffusion and filtration.

manas.q: Where is simple squamous epithelium found?

children.note: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells lines the trachea and bronchi; every cell rests on the basement membrane.

manas.q: What type of epithelium lines the trachea?

children.note: Lines the renal pelvis, ureters, bladder and proximal urethra; dome-shaped umbrella cells allow stretching.

manas.q: Which epithelium lines the urinary bladder?

children.note: Keratinised forms the epidermis; non-keratinised lines the mouth, oesophagus, vagina and ectocervix.

manas.q: Where is non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium found?

children.note: Type I: bone, tendon, ligament, dermis, scar. Type II: hyaline cartilage. Type IV: basement membranes.

manas.q: Which collagen types are found in bone, hyaline cartilage and basement membrane?

children.note: Articular surfaces, costal cartilages, tracheal rings, most laryngeal cartilages and epiphyseal growth plates; avascular.

manas.q: Name sites of hyaline cartilage.

children.note: Concentric lamellae around a central (Haversian) canal; Volkmann canals link canals; osteocytes sit in lacunae joined by canaliculi.

manas.q: What is the structural unit of compact bone?

children.note: Skeletal: striated, multinucleate, peripheral nuclei. Cardiac: striated, 1–2 central nuclei, intercalated discs. Smooth: non-striated, spindle cells.

manas.q: How do skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle differ histologically?

children.topic: 📖 4.3 Connective Tissue Supports and Protects (OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology)

children.note: The four basic tissues — epithelium, connective tissue, muscle and nerve — and how their microscopic structure fits their function.
Primary oocytes arrest in prophase I from fetal life until just before ovulation; the ovulated secondary oocyte arrests in metaphase II until fertilisation.

manas.q: At which stages of meiosis is the oocyte arrested?

children.note: Ampulla of the uterine tube, usually within about 24 hours of ovulation.

manas.q: Where does fertilisation normally occur?

children.note: Blastocyst begins implanting about day 6–7, usually in the posterior wall of the uterine body. Commonest ectopic site: ampulla of the tube.

manas.q: When and where does the blastocyst normally implant?

children.note:
Two layers (epiblast, hypoblast), two cavities (amniotic, yolk sac), two trophoblast layers (cytotrophoblast, syncytiotrophoblast).
Mnemonic: Week 2 = week of twos

manas.q: Why is week 2 called the 'week of twos'?

children.note: The syncytiotrophoblast secretes hCG, which maintains the corpus luteum and is detected by pregnancy tests.

manas.q: Which cells secrete hCG in early pregnancy?

children.note: Primitive streak forms; epiblast cells migrate through it to form the three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm.

manas.q: What process forms the three germ layers, and when?

children.note: The notochord induces the neural plate; its remnant persists as the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral discs.

manas.q: What is the adult remnant of the notochord?

children.note: Closes in week 4 (cranial neuropore ~day 25, caudal ~day 28). Failure: anencephaly or spina bifida; periconceptional folic acid lowers risk.

manas.q: When does the neural tube close and what defects follow failure?

children.note: Gametogenesis, fertilisation, implantation, the bilaminar and trilaminar disc, and neurulation.
Epidermis, hair, nails, CNS (neural tube), neural crest, lens, inner ear, anterior pituitary and tooth enamel.

manas.q: What does the ectoderm give rise to?

children.note: PNS ganglia, Schwann cells, melanocytes, adrenal medulla, most facial and skull bones, odontoblasts, aorticopulmonary septum.

manas.q: Name derivatives of the neural crest.

children.note: Muscle, bone, connective tissue, heart, vessels and blood, kidneys, gonads, spleen, adrenal cortex and serous linings.

manas.q: What does the mesoderm give rise to?

children.note: Epithelial lining of the gut and respiratory tract, liver, pancreas, thyroid follicular cells, parathyroids, thymus, bladder epithelium.

manas.q: What does the endoderm give rise to?

children.note: Arch 1: CN V (mandibular). Arch 2: CN VII. Arch 3: CN IX. Arches 4 and 6: CN X (superior and recurrent laryngeal branches).

manas.q: Which cranial nerve supplies each pharyngeal arch?

children.note: Ductus venosus → ligamentum venosum; foramen ovale → fossa ovalis; ductus arteriosus → ligamentum arteriosum.

manas.q: What are the adult remnants of the three fetal shunts?

children.note: Midgut herniates into the umbilical cord ~week 6, rotates 270° anticlockwise around the SMA and returns by ~week 10. Errors: malrotation, omphalocele.

manas.q: Describe normal midgut rotation.

children.note:
Vitelline duct remnant: ~2% of people, ~2 feet from the ileocaecal valve, ~2 inches long; may contain gastric or pancreatic tissue.
Mnemonic: Rule of 2s

manas.q: What is the 'rule of 2s' for Meckel diverticulum?

children.topic: 📖 20.6 Development of Blood Vessels and Fetal Circulation (OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology)

children.note: What each germ layer and the neural crest become, pharyngeal arches, gut rotation and fetal circulation.

Ventral rami C5–T1 form roots, trunks, divisions, cords and terminal branches.
Mnemonic: Real Teenagers Drink Cold Beer (Roots, Trunks, Divisions, Cords, Branches)

manas.q: What are the roots and parts of the brachial plexus?

children.note: Upper trunk (C5–C6) injury, e.g. shoulder dystocia: arm adducted, medially rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated ('waiter's tip').

manas.q: What are the cause and posture of Erb palsy?

children.note:
Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis. Supraspinatus is most often injured; it initiates abduction.
Mnemonic: SITS

manas.q: Name the rotator cuff muscles.

children.topic: Nerve at risk: surgical neck humerus
children.note: Axillary nerve (with posterior circumflex humeral artery): deltoid weakness and numbness over the 'regimental badge' area.

manas.q: Which nerve is injured in a surgical neck of humerus fracture?

children.note: Radial nerve in the spiral (radial) groove → wrist drop.

manas.q: Which nerve is injured in a midshaft humerus fracture and what is the sign?

children.note: Median nerve compressed under the flexor retinaculum: numbness of lateral 3½ digits, thenar wasting; palmar cutaneous branch spared.

manas.q: Which nerve is compressed in carpal tunnel syndrome and what are its signs?

children.note: Behind the medial epicondyle: weak finger ab/adduction, hypothenar wasting; clawing of ring and little fingers is milder than in wrist lesions (ulnar paradox).

manas.q: What are the signs of ulnar nerve injury at the elbow?

children.note: Scaphoid lies in its floor; tenderness suggests scaphoid fracture, which risks avascular necrosis of the proximal pole (retrograde blood supply).

manas.q: Which bone lies in the floor of the anatomical snuffbox and why does its fracture matter?

children.topic: 📖 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb (OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology)
📖 11.5 Muscles of the Pectoral Girdle and Upper Limbs (OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology)

children.note: Brachial plexus, shoulder, arm, forearm and hand, with the nerve injuries and fractures examined in clinics and OSCEs.

Bounded by inguinal ligament, sartorius (lateral) and adductor longus (medial). Lateral to medial: femoral nerve, artery, vein, lymphatics.
Mnemonic: NAVEL: Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space, Lymphatics

manas.q: What are the contents of the femoral triangle from lateral to medial?

children.note: Upper outer quadrant of the buttock (or ventrogluteal site) to avoid the sciatic nerve, which exits below piriformis.

manas.q: Where should a gluteal intramuscular injection be given and why?

children.note: L4–S3; exits the pelvis via the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis; divides into tibial and common fibular nerves above the popliteal fossa.

manas.q: What are the roots and course of the sciatic nerve?

children.note: Winds around the neck of the fibula; injured by fractures or tight casts → foot drop and numbness of the dorsum of the foot.

manas.q: Where is the common fibular nerve vulnerable and what does injury cause?

children.note: Intracapsular fracture tears retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery → avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

manas.q: Why does an intracapsular femoral neck fracture risk avascular necrosis?

children.note: Classically a lateral blow injures ACL, MCL and medial meniscus (lateral meniscus often torn too). ACL prevents anterior tibial translation (Lachman test).

manas.q: Which structures are injured in the 'unhappy triad' of the knee?

children.note: Starts anterior to the medial malleolus, ascends medially, joins the femoral vein at the saphenous opening; used for cut-down and bypass grafts.

manas.q: Describe the course of the great saphenous vein.

children.note: Anterior talofibular ligament, torn first in an inversion injury.

manas.q: Which ankle ligament is most commonly injured in an inversion sprain?

children.topic: 📖 8.4 Bones of the Lower Limb (OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology)
📖 11.6 Appendicular Muscles of the Pelvic Girdle and Lower Limbs (OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology)

children.note: Gluteal region, thigh, knee, leg and foot: nerves, vessels and joints relevant to injections, fractures and sports injuries.
7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral and about 4 coccygeal vertebrae; 31 pairs of spinal nerves.

manas.q: How many vertebrae are in each region of the spine?

children.note: C1 (atlas) has no body; C2 (axis) has the dens. Atlanto-occipital joint allows nodding ('yes'); atlanto-axial joint allows rotation ('no').

manas.q: What movements occur at the atlanto-occipital and atlanto-axial joints?

children.note: Conus medullaris ends at about L1–L2 in adults (lower, ~L3, at birth); lumbar puncture is done at L3–L4 or L4–L5.

manas.q: At what level does the adult spinal cord end?

children.note: Line joining the highest points of the iliac crests crosses the L4 spinous process or L4–L5 interspace — landmark for lumbar puncture.

manas.q: Which vertebral level does the line joining the iliac crests cross?

children.note: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura, arachnoid → subarachnoid space.

manas.q: List the layers a lumbar puncture needle passes through.

children.note: Nucleus pulposus usually herniates posterolaterally and compresses the root of the level below: L4–L5 disc → L5 root.

manas.q: Which nerve root does a posterolateral L4–L5 disc herniation compress?

children.note: Dorsal columns (fine touch, vibration, proprioception) cross in the medulla; spinothalamic tract (pain, temperature) crosses near its entry segment.

manas.q: Where do the dorsal column and spinothalamic pathways decussate?

children.note: Cord hemisection: ipsilateral weakness and loss of vibration/proprioception; contralateral loss of pain and temperature below the lesion.

manas.q: What are the features of Brown-Séquard syndrome?

children.topic: 📖 13.2 The Central Nervous System (OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology)

children.note: Vertebral column, spinal cord and its tracts, and the anatomy behind lumbar puncture and disc disease.
At T4/T5 level: 2nd costal cartilage, tracheal bifurcation, start and end of the aortic arch, boundary of superior and inferior mediastinum.

manas.q: What structures lie at the level of the sternal angle?

children.note:
Runs in the costal groove below each rib, vein–artery–nerve from above down; so insert needles and drains just above the lower rib.
Mnemonic: VAN (vein, artery, nerve from above down)

manas.q: Why are chest drains inserted just above a rib?

children.note: Anterior border of latissimus dorsi, lateral border of pectoralis major, horizontal line at nipple level (5th intercostal space), apex below axilla.

manas.q: What are the boundaries of the safe triangle for chest drain insertion?

children.note: Right lung: 3 lobes (oblique and horizontal fissures). Left lung: 2 lobes, with lingula and cardiac notch.

manas.q: How many lobes does each lung have?

children.note: Right main bronchus — it is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left.

manas.q: Into which bronchus are foreign bodies usually aspirated, and why?

children.note:
IVC at T8, oesophagus at T10, aorta at T12.
Mnemonic: I 8 10 Eggs At 12 (IVC 8, Oesophagus 10, Aorta 12)

manas.q: At which vertebral levels do the IVC, oesophagus and aorta pass through the diaphragm?

children.note:
C3–C5; the only motor supply to the diaphragm; diaphragmatic irritation refers pain to the shoulder tip.
Mnemonic: C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive

manas.q: What are the roots of the phrenic nerve?

children.note: Lung: rib 6 (midclavicular), 8 (midaxillary), 10 (posteriorly). Pleura is two ribs lower: 8, 10, 12.

manas.q: What are the surface markings of the lower borders of the lung and pleura?

children.note: Ribs, intercostal spaces, diaphragm, pleura and lungs — the anatomy behind chest drains, auscultation and aspiration.
Which artery gives the posterior interventricular (descending) artery; most people are right dominant.

manas.q: How is coronary artery dominance defined?

children.note: Supplies anterior left ventricle, anterior two-thirds of the septum and apex; the most commonly occluded coronary artery.

manas.q: What does the left anterior descending artery supply?

children.note: Wall of the right atrium near the opening of the SVC; supplied by the right coronary artery in most people.

manas.q: Where is the SA node and which artery usually supplies it?

children.note: Right border: right atrium. Left border: left ventricle and left auricle. Inferior border: mainly right ventricle.

manas.q: Which chambers form the right and left borders of the heart?

children.note: Left atrium, lying against the oesophagus; enlargement (e.g. mitral stenosis) can cause dysphagia; well seen on transoesophageal echo.

manas.q: Which chamber of the heart is most posterior?

children.note: Aortic: right 2nd ICS. Pulmonary: left 2nd ICS. Tricuspid: left lower sternal edge. Mitral: apex, left 5th ICS midclavicular line.

manas.q: Where are the four valve auscultation areas?

children.note: Mitral valve (then aortic). Rheumatic heart disease follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis and remains common in Kenya.

manas.q: Which valve is most commonly affected in rheumatic heart disease?

children.note: Fluid in the pericardial sac restricts filling. Beck triad: hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds. Pericardiocentesis via subxiphoid route.

manas.q: What is Beck triad?

children.topic: 📖 19.5 Development of the Heart (OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology)

children.note: Pericardium, chambers, valves, coronary circulation and conducting system, with surface anatomy for examination.
Midway between jugular notch and pubic symphysis: pylorus, pancreatic neck, renal hila, gallbladder fundus, end of spinal cord.

manas.q: Which structures lie on the transpyloric plane?

children.note: Formed by two midclavicular lines and the subcostal and transtubercular planes: hypochondria, epigastric, flanks, umbilical, iliac fossae, hypogastric.

manas.q: Which lines and planes divide the abdomen into nine regions?

children.note: About 4 cm from deep ring (lateral to inferior epigastric vessels) to superficial ring; carries spermatic cord or round ligament and ilioinguinal nerve.

manas.q: What passes through the inguinal canal?

children.note:
Indirect: via deep ring, lateral to inferior epigastric vessels, patent processus vaginalis. Direct: through Hesselbach triangle, medial to them.
Mnemonic: MDs don't LIe: Medial Direct, Lateral Indirect

manas.q: How are direct and indirect inguinal hernias distinguished anatomically?

children.note: Inferior epigastric vessels (lateral), lateral border of rectus abdominis (medial), inguinal ligament (inferior).

manas.q: What are the boundaries of Hesselbach triangle?

children.note: Through the femoral canal, below and lateral to the pubic tubercle; more common in women and has a high risk of strangulation.

manas.q: Where does a femoral hernia emerge relative to the pubic tubercle?

children.note: Links greater and lesser sacs; its anterior wall is the hepatoduodenal ligament with the portal triad (compressed in the Pringle manoeuvre).

manas.q: What forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen?

children.note:
Adrenals, aorta/IVC, duodenum (parts 2–4), pancreas (not tail), ureters, ascending and descending colon, kidneys, oesophagus (lower), rectum.
Mnemonic: SAD PUCKER

manas.q: List the retroperitoneal organs.

children.topic: 📖 11.4 Axial Muscles of the Abdominal Wall, and Thorax (OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology)

children.note: Abdominal regions and planes, inguinal canal and hernias, and the peritoneal cavity and its folds.
Left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries; supply the foregut to the 2nd part of duodenum, liver, spleen and part of pancreas.

manas.q: What are the three branches of the coeliac trunk?

children.note: SMA: midgut, from 2nd part of duodenum to proximal two-thirds of transverse colon. IMA: hindgut, to upper anal canal.

manas.q: Which parts of the gut do the SMA and IMA supply?

children.note: Lower oesophagus (varices), anorectum, paraumbilical (caput medusae), retroperitoneum. Schistosoma mansoni is a key cause of portal hypertension in Kenya.

manas.q: Where are the portosystemic anastomoses?

children.note: Cystic duct, common hepatic duct and inferior liver border; contains the cystic artery, identified during cholecystectomy.

manas.q: What are the boundaries and key content of Calot triangle?

children.note: One-third of the way from the ASIS to the umbilicus; surface marking of the appendix base. Commonest appendix position: retrocaecal.

manas.q: Where is McBurney point?
